lessons.title: Understanding Electrical Circuits and Solar Wiring
lessons.body:
In a solar system, electricity flows in a closed loop called a circuit. Think of it like water in a pipe: the solar panel is the pump, wires are pipes, and the load (like a light bulb) is a water wheel. Current (measured in amps) is the flow rate, voltage (volts) is the pressure, and resistance (ohms) slows the flow. In Africa, we often use 12V or 24V DC systems for small homes. A basic circuit has a power source (solar panel), a conductor (copper wire), a load (appliance), and a switch or controller to turn it on and off.

Wiring must be sized correctly. If a wire is too thin, it heats up and wastes power, or even starts a fire. Use this rule: for every 10 amps of current, use at least 2.5 mmÂ² copper wire for short runs (under 5 meters). For longer runs, go thicker. For example, a 100W solar panel at 12V produces about 8.3 amps. A 2.5 mmÂ² wire is fine for a 3-meter cable from panel to charge controller. Always use stranded copper wire for solar, not solid, because it bends easier and handles vibration.

Connections must be tight. Loose connections cause resistance, heat, and voltage drop. Use proper MC4 connectors for solar panelsâthey click and lock, and are waterproof. For other connections, use terminal blocks or crimp connectors with a crimping tool. Never twist wires together and tape them; that fails in heat and humidity. In many African communities, we see burnt wires from poor connections. Strip only 1 cm of insulation, insert into connector, and crimp firmly. Tug test: pull gently to ensure it holds.

Safety first: always disconnect the solar panel or battery before working. Use insulated tools. DC electricity can arc more than AC, so never work live. A simple multimeter (cost about 10,000 Naira or 200 KES) is your best friendâmeasure voltage and continuity. Remember, a solar circuit is only as strong as its weakest connection.

lessons.title: Connecting Solar Panels in Series and Parallel
lessons.body:
Solar panels can be wired in series or parallel to get the voltage and current you need. Series means connecting the positive of one panel to the negative of the next. This adds voltages. For example, two 12V panels in series give 24V, but the current stays the same (say 5A). Parallel means connecting all positives together and all negatives together. This adds currents. Two 12V panels in parallel give 12V but double the current (10A).

Why choose one over the other? If you have a 24V battery bank and a 24V charge controller, you need at least 24V from panels. Two 12V panels in series works. If you have a 12V system and want to charge faster, parallel gives more current. But higher current means thicker wires. Series is often better for long distances because higher voltage suffers less voltage drop. However, series has a drawback: if one panel is shaded, the whole string drops. In parallel, only the shaded panel drops.

Use MC4 connectors for easy series/parallel. For series, plug the positive MC4 of panel 1 into the negative MC4 of panel 2. For parallel, you need branch connectors (Y-connectors) to join positives together and negatives together. Always check polarity with a multimeter before connecting to the controller. Reverse polarity can destroy equipment.

Real example: You have four 100W panels, each 12V, 8.3A. To make a 24V system, connect two pairs in series (each pair gives 24V, 8.3A), then connect the two pairs in parallel (gives 24V, 16.6A). That's 400W total. Use 4 mmÂ² wire for the parallel connections and 6 mmÂ² for the run to the controller if over 5 meters. Always mount panels facing the equator (north in southern Africa, south in northern Africa) at an angle equal to your latitude. Keep connections off the ground and waterproof with self-amalgamating tape.

lessons.title: Wiring Inverters and Charge Controllers
lessons.body:
The charge controller sits between solar panels and battery. It prevents overcharging and reverse current at night. There are two types: PWM (cheap, less efficient) and MPPT (expensive, 30% more power). For a small home, a 30A PWM controller costs about 15,000 Naira or 3,000 KES. Connect panels to controller first, then controller to battery. Never connect battery firstâit can damage the controller. Use thick wire: for 30A, use 6 mmÂ². Keep cable runs short.

The inverter changes DC battery power to AC for appliances like TVs, fridges, or phone chargers. Inverters come in 12V, 24V, or 48V input. Match inverter voltage to battery bank. A 1000W inverter can run a small fridge (200W) and lights. Connect inverter directly to battery with thick cablesâat least 16 mmÂ² for 1000W at 12V (which draws about 83A). Use a fuse or circuit breaker on the positive cable within 30 cm of the battery. A 100A fuse is typical. Never use car jumper cables; they are too thin and will melt.

Wiring order for safety: First, connect charge controller to battery (with a fuse). Then connect solar panels to controller. Then connect inverter to battery. When disconnecting, reverse: inverter off, then panels, then controller, then battery. Always use a multimeter to check voltage at each step. For example, battery should read 12.6V for a full 12V battery. Controller output should be slightly higher when charging. Inverter output should be 220V-240V AC. If you see smoke or smell burning, disconnect immediately. Use conduit or cable ties to keep wires neat and away from water. In rural areas, protect from rats and termites by using metal conduit.

lessons.title: Battery Bank Wiring and Safety
lessons.body:
Batteries store energy for night and cloudy days. Most solar systems use deep-cycle lead-acid or lithium batteries. Lead-acid is cheaper but heavier and needs maintenance. Lithium (LiFePO4) lasts longer but costs more. A 12V 100Ah lead-acid battery stores about 1.2 kWh, but only use 50% (0.6 kWh) to prolong life. So a 100W light for 6 hours uses 0.6 kWhâone battery.

You can wire batteries in series to increase voltage or parallel to increase capacity. Series: positive of battery 1 to negative of battery 2 gives 24V. Parallel: all positives together, all negatives together gives 12V but double Ah. For a 24V system, use two 12V batteries in series. For more capacity, add another pair in parallel. Always use identical batteries: same brand, age, and capacity. Mixing old and new causes imbalance and early failure.

Use thick cables: for a 12V 100Ah battery, inverter cables should be at least 16 mmÂ² if under 1 meter. For longer, go thicker. Connect batteries with short, equal-length cables to keep resistance balanced. Use ring terminals crimped or soldered. Never connect positive to negative directlyâthat's a short circuit and can explode. Install a fuse on the main positive cable. A 100A fuse for a 1000W inverter. Also, use a battery monitor to check state of charge.

Safety: Batteries produce explosive hydrogen gas when charging. Keep them in a ventilated box, not in living spaces. Wear gloves and goggles. Avoid sparks. Use a wrench with insulated handle. In Africa, heat shortens battery lifeâkeep them shaded and cool. Check water levels in lead-acid monthly (if flooded). For lithium, no water needed. Always disconnect the negative first when removing a battery. A well-wired battery bank can last 5-7 years; a poorly wired one fails in months.

lessons.title: Grounding and Bonding Solar Systems
lessons.body:
Grounding protects you and your equipment from electric shock and lightning. It creates a safe path for fault current to go into the earth. In a solar system, you need to ground the solar panel frames, charge controller, inverter, and battery negative (for negative-ground systems). Use a copper-clad ground rod, 2 meters long, driven into moist soil. If soil is dry, use two rods 2 meters apart. Connect them with 6 mmÂ² bare copper wire.

Bonding means connecting all metal parts together so they are at the same voltage. This prevents sparks. For example, bond the solar panel frames to each other with 6 mmÂ² green/yellow wire. Then run a single wire to the ground rod. Also bond the inverter case, controller case, and battery rack. Use proper ground lugs and stainless steel bolts. Never use aluminum wire for groundingâit corrodes.

In areas with frequent lightning, like many parts of Africa, add a lightning arrestor (surge protector) on the DC side and AC side. A DC surge protector costs about 20,000 Naira or 4,000 KES. Connect it between positive and negative, and to ground. For AC, use a surge protector in the distribution box. Grounding also reduces radio interference and stabilizes voltage.

Test grounding with a multimeter: set to continuity, touch one probe to ground rod and the other to a panel frame. It should beep. If not, check connections. A good ground resistance is under 25 ohms. You can measure with a ground resistance tester, but a cheap method: use a multimeter on resistance, but it's not accurate. For most small systems, if you have a solid connection, it's fine. Remember, grounding is not optionalâit saves lives. In many African installations, lack of grounding causes fires during lightning storms. So always drive that rod deep.

lessons.title: Testing Electrical Connections
lessons.body:
Testing ensures your wiring is safe and works. You need a digital multimeter (DMM). A basic one costs 10,000 Naira or 2,000 KES. It measures voltage (V), current (A), resistance (ohms), and continuity. Before testing, disconnect power. For continuity, set DMM to beep mode. Touch probes togetherâit beeps. Then test each wire: from one end to the other, it should beep. If not, the wire is broken. Test connections: a loose connection will not beep or will show high resistance.

To test voltage, set DMM to DC volts (Vâ). For a 12V battery, touch red probe to positive, black to negative. A full battery reads 12.6V. If below 11.8V, it's discharged. For solar panel, in full sun, a 12V panel should read about 18V open-circuit. If it reads 0V, check connections or panel. For AC inverter output, set to AC volts (V~). Should read 220-240V. If not, check inverter.

To test current, you need to break the circuit and put DMM in series. Most DMMs have a 10A limit. For higher current, use a clamp meter. A clamp meter costs about 25,000 Naira or 5,000 KES. Clamp around the positive wire to read amps. For a 100W panel, you should see about 5-6A in full sun. If lower, check for shading or dirty panels.

Also test for short circuits: set DMM to resistance. Touch probes to positive and negative of a circuit (with power off). It should read infinite (OL). If it reads 0 ohms, there's a short. Fix before powering. Test insulation: use a megohmmeter (if available) to check for leaks to ground. For most community installs, a visual inspection and DMM are enough. Always test after installation and every 6 months. Keep a log of readings. If you find a hot connection (feel with back of handâcareful), tighten or re-crimp. A good connection is cool and tight.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Electrical Wiring and Connections for Solar Installations in Africa

This practical reference is for technicians, installers, and small business owners delivering solar solutions in African communities. It consolidates the key wiring principles from the module into a single, field-ready guide. Whether you are wiring a 3 kW home system in Kenya, a 5 kW shop in Nigeria, or a mini-grid in Tanzania, the rules of electrical circuits, series/parallel connections, inverter and charge controller wiring, battery safety, grounding, and testing remain the same. Master these, and you reduce callbacks, protect your reputation, and build a profitable solar business.

1. Understanding Electrical Circuits and Solar Wiring

A solar electric system is a set of circuits: DC circuits from panels to charge controller, DC circuits from controller to battery, and AC circuits from inverter to loads. Every circuit needs a closed loop, a protective device (fuse or breaker), and correct polarity. In African installations, voltage drop is a common hidden cost. Keep DC cable runs short and size conductors to limit voltage drop to under 3% for critical systems. Use UV-resistant, double-insulated solar cable (e.g., 4 mmÂ² or 6 mmÂ²) and avoid joining cables with tape; use proper MC4 connectors or junction boxes.

2. Connecting Solar Panels in Series and Parallel

Series wiring adds voltage; parallel wiring adds current. For a 24 V battery bank, two 12 V panels in series give 24 V and are ideal for long cable runs. For a 12 V system with two 12 V panels, parallel keeps voltage at 12 V but doubles current; use thicker cable. Never mix different panel models in the same stringâmismatch reduces output. In dusty or hot African conditions, leave a 10â15 cm gap between panels for airflow and use bypass diodes to limit shading losses.

3. Wiring Inverters and Charge Controllers

Connect the charge controller to the battery first, then to the solar array. This lets the controller sense battery voltage and avoid damage. For inverters, use a DC breaker between battery and inverter, and an AC breaker on the output. Size cables for the inverter's continuous power: a 1 kW inverter at 12 V draws about 83 A, so use at least 25 mmÂ² copper cable for short runs. In many African markets, pure sine wave inverters are essential for fridges, TVs, and phone chargers. Always follow the manufacturer's torque specs on terminalsâloose connections cause fires.

4. Battery Bank Wiring and Safety

Batteries are the most dangerous part of a solar system. Series connections increase voltage; parallel connections increase capacity. For a 24 V 200 Ah bank, use two 12 V 200 Ah batteries in series. For 400 Ah at 12 V, use two 12 V 200 Ah in parallel. Use identical batteries (same age, type, capacity). Install in a ventilated, locked box; lead-acid batteries emit hydrogen. In hot climates, keep batteries shaded; high temperature shortens life. Use insulated tools and remove metal jewellery.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING: Never short-circuit battery terminals. A 12 V lead-acid battery can deliver hundreds of amps, causing burns, fire, or explosion. Always disconnect the negative terminal first and reconnect it last. Use fuses within 30 cm of the battery positive terminal. In case of acid spill, flush with clean water for 15 minutes and seek medical help.

5. Grounding and Bonding Solar Systems

Grounding protects people and equipment from lightning and faults. In Africa, lightning is a major risk. Ground the panel frames, mounting rails, inverter case, and charge controller case to a common earth electrode (copper rod driven 1.5â2 m into moist soil). Use green/yellow insulated cable of at least 6 mmÂ². Bond all metal parts together. For off-grid systems, do not bond DC negative to earth unless the inverter requires it. Test earth resistance; aim for less than 5 ohms. If soil is dry, use multiple rods or chemical earthing compounds.

6. Testing Electrical Connections

Before powering up, test every connection. Use a multimeter to check polarity, continuity, and voltage. Measure open-circuit voltage (Voc) of the array and compare to expected. Check short-circuit current (Isc) with a clamp meter. Verify battery voltage and specific gravity (for flooded batteries). After power-up, measure voltage drop under load. Thermographic cameras or IR thermometers can spot hot joints. Keep a log for every installationâthis is your business quality record.

quiz.q: What is the main function of a charge controller in a solar system?
options: C) Prevent battery overcharge and reverse current
quiz.explanation: The charge controller regulates voltage and current from panels to battery, preventing overcharge and reverse flow at night.

quiz.q: Which wire size is recommended for a 10 amp current over a short run?
quiz.explanation: For every 10 amps, at least 2.5 mmÂ² copper wire is needed for short runs to avoid overheating.

quiz.q: What happens to voltage and current when two 12V solar panels are connected in series?
options: B) Voltage doubles to 24V, current stays same
C) Both voltage and current double
quiz.explanation: In series, voltages add while current remains the same.

quiz.q: Why is stranded copper wire preferred over solid wire for solar installations?
options: C) It bends easier and resists vibration
quiz.explanation: Stranded wire is more flexible and durable in outdoor conditions with movement.

quiz.q: What is the correct wiring order when connecting a solar system?
options: A) Battery to controller, then panels, then inverter
B) Panels to controller, then battery, then inverter
C) Inverter to battery, then controller, then panels
D) Panels to inverter, then controller, then battery
quiz.explanation: Connect battery to controller first to allow controller to sense voltage, then panels, then inverter.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a fuse in a battery cable?
options: B) To protect against short circuits and overcurrent
D) To convert AC to DC
quiz.explanation: A fuse melts and breaks the circuit if current exceeds safe limits, preventing fire.

quiz.q: What is the recommended depth for a ground rod?
quiz.explanation: A 2-meter copper-clad ground rod is standard for good earthing in most soils.

quiz.q: Which multimeter setting is used to check if a wire is broken?
quiz.explanation: Continuity mode beeps if there is a complete path, indicating the wire is not broken.

quiz.q: What is the typical open-circuit voltage of a 12V solar panel in full sun?
quiz.explanation: A nominal 12V panel produces about 18V open-circuit, which drops under load.

quiz.q: Why should you never mix old and new batteries in a bank?
options: A) They will not fit together
B) They cause imbalance and early failure
C) They produce too much voltage
quiz.explanation: Different internal resistances cause unequal charging and discharging, damaging the bank.

quiz.q: What does a clamp meter measure?
options: B) Current without breaking the circuit
quiz.explanation: A clamp meter clamps around a wire to measure current via magnetic field.

quiz.q: What is the danger of loose electrical connections?
options: B) They cause resistance, heat, and voltage drop
D) They are safe if taped
quiz.explanation: Loose connections have high resistance, generating heat that can melt insulation or cause fire.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of MPPT charge controller over PWM?
options: B) More efficient, up to 30% more power
quiz.explanation: MPPT tracks maximum power point, converting excess voltage to extra current.

quiz.q: When disconnecting a solar system, what is the correct order?
options: A) Battery first, then panels, then controller
B) Inverter off, then panels, then controller, then battery
C) Panels first, then battery, then inverter
D) Controller first, then inverter, then battery
quiz.explanation: Turn off inverter, disconnect panels from controller, then controller from battery to avoid sparks.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of bonding in a solar system?
options: B) To connect all metal parts to the same voltage
D) To convert DC to AC
quiz.explanation: Bonding equalizes potential between metal parts, preventing sparks and shocks.

quiz.q: Which tool is essential for making secure crimp connections?
quiz.explanation: A crimping tool compresses the connector onto the wire for a tight, reliable joint.

quiz.q: What should you do if a battery is swollen or leaking?
quiz.explanation: Swollen or leaking batteries are damaged and dangerous; replace them.

quiz.q: What is the typical AC output voltage of a solar inverter for home use?
quiz.explanation: Most African countries use 220-240V AC for household appliances.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep solar panels clean?
options: A) To make them look nice
B) To prevent dust from reducing current output
quiz.explanation: Dust and dirt block sunlight, reducing current and power production.

quiz.q: What is the maximum current a typical multimeter can measure directly?
quiz.explanation: Most handheld multimeters have a 10A limit; higher currents need a clamp meter.

quiz.q: What is the first step before working on any solar electrical circuit?
quiz.explanation: Always disconnect power sources to avoid shock or damage.

quiz.q: What does a reading of 'OL' on a multimeter in resistance mode mean?
quiz.explanation: OL indicates no continuity, meaning the circuit is open or broken.

quiz.q: Which of these is a correct method for connecting solar panels in parallel?
options: A) Positive to negative of next panel
B) All positives together, all negatives together
C) Positive to positive and negative to negative of same panel
quiz.explanation: Parallel connection joins all positives and all negatives, increasing current.

quiz.q: What is the recommended fuse size for a 1000W inverter at 12V?
quiz.explanation: 1000W at 12V draws about 83A, so a 100A fuse is appropriate.

quiz.q: Why should batteries be kept in a ventilated area?
options: B) To release explosive hydrogen gas
quiz.explanation: Charging batteries produce hydrogen gas, which can explode if trapped.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a surge protector in a solar system?
options: B) To protect against lightning and voltage spikes
D) To convert DC to AC
quiz.explanation: Surge protectors divert excess voltage from lightning or switching transients to ground.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to strip wire for a connection?
options: B) Use a wire stripper to remove 1 cm
D) Cut with a knife at an angle
quiz.explanation: A wire stripper cleanly removes insulation without nicking the copper.

quiz.q: What does a battery monitor measure?
quiz.explanation: A battery monitor tracks voltage and current to estimate remaining capacity.

quiz.q: Why is it important to use identical cables for parallel battery connections?
quiz.explanation: Equal cable lengths ensure equal current sharing and balanced charging.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to check if a solar panel produces no voltage?
options: B) Check connections and multimeter settings
quiz.explanation: Often the issue is a loose connection or wrong multimeter setting, not a faulty panel.
